title: MicroRNA in Glioblastoma: A Comprehensive Survey of Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Therapeutic Implications

subsections.section_title: Biological Roles of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
subsections.subsection_title: Oncogenic microRNAs (oncomiRs) in glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Oncogenic microRNAs (oncomiRs) play a pivotal role in glioblastoma pathogenesis by promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation, inhibiting apoptosis, and enhancing tumor aggressiveness. MiR-21 is one of the most consistently upregulated oncomiRs in glioblastoma, where it targets tumor suppressors such as PTEN and PDCD4, thereby activating PI3K/AKT and MAPK signaling pathways to drive tumor growth [1]. Similarly, miR-10b is overexpressed in glioblastoma stem cells and promotes invasion by repressing HOXD10 and activating RHOC, contributing to mesenchymal transition [2]. MiR-221 and miR-222 are co-expressed and enhance proliferation by downregulating the cell cycle inhibitors p27Kip1 and p57Kip2, while also conferring resistance to temozolomide [3]. MiR-155 promotes gliomagenesis by suppressing SOCS1, leading to hyperactivation of STAT3 signaling and increased inflammatory tumor microenvironment cues [4]. Additionally, miR-17-92 cluster members, particularly miR-19a and miR-19b, inhibit PTEN and BIM expression, synergistically enhancing survival and proliferation [5].

Emerging evidence implicates miR-106b-25 cluster members in glioblastoma progression by targeting E2F1 regulators and BIM, thereby suppressing apoptosis [6]. MiR-93, a member of the miR-106b-25 cluster, also promotes angiogenesis by targeting integrin-β8 and VEGF inhibitors [7]. MiR-125b is upregulated in recurrent glioblastoma and enhances stemness and therapy resistance by repressing TP53INP1 and LIN28B [8]. These oncomiRs often act in concert, forming regulatory networks that reinforce oncogenic signaling and adapt to therapeutic pressure, making them attractive but complex therapeutic targets [9].

subsections.section_title: Biological Roles of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
subsections.subsection_title: Tumor-suppressive microRNAs and their silencing
subsections.content:
Numerous microRNAs function as tumor suppressors in glioblastoma by targeting oncogenic pathways involved in proliferation, survival, and invasion. For instance, miR-128 represses BMI1 and E2F3, thereby inhibiting cell cycle progression and inducing differentiation in glioma cells [1]. Similarly, miR-34a directly targets NOTCH1 and MET, suppressing stemness and tumorigenic potential in glioblastoma stem cells [2]. Loss of miR-181 family members, which normally inhibit BCL2 and MCL1, contributes to apoptosis evasion and chemoresistance [3]. These tumor-suppressive miRNAs are frequently silenced through epigenetic mechanisms, including promoter hypermethylation and histone deacetylation, as demonstrated for miR-124 and miR-137, both of which are downregulated in glioblastoma due to CpG island methylation [4].

Additionally, miR-7 targets EGFR and IRS-1/2, disrupting key signaling cascades driving glioblastoma growth; its expression is suppressed by the transcription factor YY1 and by RNA-binding proteins that destabilize its transcript [5]. miR-145, another potent suppressor, inhibits OCT4 and SOX2, thereby impairing stem cell maintenance, and is silenced via promoter methylation and transcriptional repression by c-MYC [6]. The silencing of miR-146a, which negatively regulates IRAK1 and TRAF6 to dampen NF-κB signaling, further promotes an inflammatory tumor microenvironment [7]. Collectively, these findings underscore that the functional loss of tumor-suppressive miRNAs is a hallmark of glioblastoma pathogenesis, driven by both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms that disrupt critical regulatory networks.

subsections.section_title: Biological Roles of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
subsections.subsection_title: Regulation of glioma stem cells by microRNAs
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs play a pivotal role in maintaining the stem-like properties of glioma stem cells (GSCs), which are critical for tumor initiation, therapy resistance, and recurrence. The miR-128 family has been shown to suppress GSC self-renewal by targeting key stemness regulators such as BMI1 and E2F3, thereby promoting differentiation and reducing tumorigenic potential. Similarly, miR-34a directly inhibits NOTCH1 and MET, two central nodes in GSC maintenance pathways, leading to diminished sphere formation and enhanced sensitivity to radiation. In contrast, miR-10b is upregulated in GSCs and promotes stemness by repressing HOXD10, thereby enhancing invasiveness and self-renewal capacity. Additionally, miR-125b sustains GSC populations by downregulating TP53INP1 and LIN28B, which otherwise restrict stem cell expansion and promote differentiation.

Epigenetic silencing of miR-124 and miR-137, previously implicated in glioblastoma pathogenesis, also contributes to GSC maintenance by derepressing stem cell factors such as SOX2 and SLIT2. Furthermore, miR-145, though silenced by c-MYC, directly targets OCT4 and SOX2, and its restoration suppresses GSC self-renewal. The miR-17-92 cluster, while primarily known for targeting PTEN and BIM, also enhances GSC proliferation by modulating the PTEN/AKT axis and suppressing p21 expression. Finally, miR-21, overexpressed in GSCs, supports stemness by inhibiting PDCD4 and PTEN, thereby activating pro-survival signaling cascades that sustain the undifferentiated state.

subsections.section_title: Biological Roles of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA-mediated modulation of the tumor microenvironment
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs play a critical role in shaping the glioblastoma tumor microenvironment (TME) by modulating communication between tumor cells and non-neoplastic stromal components, including microglia, macrophages, astrocytes, and endothelial cells. Tumor-derived exosomal miR-21 is taken up by macrophages, promoting their polarization toward an M2 immunosuppressive phenotype, thereby facilitating immune evasion and tumor progression [1]. Similarly, miR-1246 secreted by glioblastoma cells reprograms tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) via the TLR4/NF-κB pathway, enhancing pro-tumorigenic cytokine secretion [2]. In addition, miR-155 overexpression in glioblastoma-derived extracellular vesicles induces pro-inflammatory activation of microglia, contributing to a chronic inflammatory milieu that supports invasion [3].

Conversely, loss of tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-146a in glioblastoma cells leads to elevated expression of IRAK1 and TRAF6, amplifying NF-κB-driven inflammation and recruiting immunosuppressive myeloid cells [4]. Endothelial cells within the TME are also targeted by glioblastoma-secreted miRNAs; for instance, miR-93 suppresses integrin-β8 and VEGF inhibitors in endothelial cells, promoting angiogenesis and vascular abnormality [5]. Furthermore, miR-296 has been shown to enhance vascular permeability by downregulating HGS, facilitating tumor cell intravasation [6]. Astrocytes, when exposed to glioblastoma-derived miR-19a, upregulate IL-6 and CCL2, creating a neuroinflammatory niche that supports tumor survival [7]. These findings underscore the bidirectional miRNA-mediated crosstalk that reprograms the TME into a pro-tumorigenic ecosystem.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation: Molecular Mechanisms and Epigenetic Control
subsections.subsection_title: Genomic deletions, amplifications, and mutations affecting microRNA loci
subsections.content:
Genomic alterations, including deletions, amplifications, and point mutations, frequently disrupt microRNA loci in glioblastoma, leading to widespread dysregulation of tumor-suppressive and oncogenic miRNAs. Recurrent homozygous deletions at chromosome 13q14.3 encompassing the miR-15a/16-1 cluster are associated with loss of tumor suppression and enhanced cell survival in glioblastoma, as these miRNAs target BCL2 and CCND1 [1]. Similarly, deletion of the miR-34a locus at 1p36.23, a p53-regulated tumor suppressor, is observed in a subset of glioblastomas and correlates with impaired apoptosis and stem cell maintenance [2]. Conversely, amplification of the miR-17-92 cluster on 13q31.3 is prevalent in glioblastoma and drives proliferation by repressing PTEN, BIM, and E2F1 [3]. Point mutations within the seed regions of miR-128 and miR-145 have been identified in glioblastoma genomes, impairing their ability to regulate target mRNAs involved in stemness and differentiation [4]. Additionally, structural variants such as chromosomal translocations have been reported to reposition miR-21 into enhancer-rich regions, contributing to its aberrant overexpression independent of transcriptional activation [5].

Whole-genome sequencing studies have further revealed somatic mutations in the promoter regions of miR-124 and miR-137, reducing their transcriptional activity despite intact genomic copy number [6]. Copy number gains at 14q32.31, harboring the DLK1-DIO3 imprinted cluster including miR-134 and miR-485, are linked to enhanced invasion and therapy resistance [7]. Mutations in the 3'UTRs of miRNA host genes, such as MIR17HG, can alter miRNA processing efficiency by disrupting Drosha/DGCR8 recognition sites [8]. These genomic lesions collectively contribute to the rewiring of miRNA regulatory networks in glioblastoma, establishing a foundation for tumor heterogeneity and therapeutic evasion.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation: Molecular Mechanisms and Epigenetic Control
subsections.subsection_title: Epigenetic silencing via DNA methylation and histone modification
subsections.content:
Epigenetic silencing of tumor-suppressive microRNAs in glioblastoma is frequently mediated by promoter DNA hypermethylation and repressive histone modifications. The miR-124 and miR-137 loci are among the most commonly methylated in glioblastoma, leading to transcriptional repression and loss of their neurodifferentiation-promoting functions. This silencing is associated with increased expression of stemness factors such as SOX2 and CDK6, contributing to tumor aggressiveness and therapy resistance. Similarly, miR-128 and miR-145 are suppressed via CpG island methylation and H3K27me3 enrichment, impairing their ability to target oncogenes like BMI1 and OCT4. The polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), through EZH2-mediated H3K27 trimethylation, plays a central role in this repression, with EZH2 overexpression correlating with poor prognosis in glioblastoma patients.

Histone deacetylase (HDAC) activity further contributes to miRNA silencing by compacting chromatin at miRNA promoters. Inhibition of HDACs restores expression of miR-34a and miR-145, demonstrating the reversibility of epigenetic repression. Additionally, the miR-181 family is silenced by coordinated DNA methylation and H3K9me3 marks in glioblastoma stem cells, promoting chemoresistance. These epigenetic alterations often occur independently of genomic deletions or mutations, highlighting their role as primary drivers of miRNA dysregulation. The interplay between DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA networks creates a self-reinforcing oncogenic state that sustains glioblastoma stemness and progression.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation: Molecular Mechanisms and Epigenetic Control
subsections.subsection_title: Dysregulation of microRNA biogenesis machinery
subsections.content:
Dysregulation of the microRNA biogenesis machinery is a hallmark of glioblastoma, contributing to global miRNA imbalance through altered expression of key processing enzymes. Drosha and Dicer, essential for pri-miRNA and pre-miRNA cleavage, are frequently downregulated in glioblastoma, leading to reduced mature miRNA levels and loss of tumor-suppressive functions. Reduced Dicer expression correlates with poor prognosis and enhanced stemness, as demonstrated in patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells ref [39]. Similarly, DGCR8, a critical component of the Microprocessor complex, is suppressed by oncogenic signaling pathways, impairing pri-miRNA processing ref [40]. The RNA-binding protein LIN28B, overexpressed in glioblastoma, binds to let-7 family precursors and blocks their maturation, promoting stem cell maintenance and chemoresistance ref [41]. Furthermore, mutations in genes encoding exportin-5 (XPO5) disrupt nuclear export of pre-miRNAs, resulting in cytoplasmic depletion of mature miRNAs ref [42]. Post-transcriptional modifications, such as adenosine-to-inosine editing by ADAR enzymes, can alter miRNA seed sequences and target specificity, contributing to oncogenic reprogramming ref [43].

Additional layers of dysregulation arise from aberrant expression of auxiliary factors such as TRBP and PACT, which stabilize Dicer and facilitate RISC loading; their downregulation in glioblastoma impairs miRNA function even when precursor levels are intact ref [44]. Notably, the oncoprotein c-MYC transcriptionally represses Dicer and Drosha, creating a feed-forward loop that suppresses tumor-suppressive miRNAs while promoting proliferation ref [45]. Recent studies also implicate the ubiquitin-proteasome system in the degradation of Dicer and Drosha proteins, with E3 ligases such as TRIM25 being upregulated in glioblastoma to accelerate their turnover ref [46]. Collectively, these defects in the miRNA biogenesis pathway represent a non-genomic, yet highly recurrent, mechanism of miRNA dysregulation that synergizes with epigenetic and genomic alterations to drive glioblastoma pathogenesis.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation: Molecular Mechanisms and Epigenetic Control
subsections.subsection_title: Transcription factor networks controlling microRNA expression
subsections.content:
Transcription factor networks play a central role in orchestrating microRNA expression in glioblastoma, often acting as master regulators that either activate oncogenic miRNAs or repress tumor-suppressive ones. The oncogenic transcription factor c-MYC directly binds to promoters of the miR-17-92 cluster and represses tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-145 and miR-128, thereby promoting proliferation and stemness [1]. Similarly, NF-κB activates miR-21 and miR-155 expression, enhancing inflammation, survival, and therapy resistance in glioblastoma cells [2]. Conversely, p53 transcriptionally induces miR-34a and miR-145, both of which are frequently silenced in glioblastoma, contributing to unchecked stem cell self-renewal [3]. The zinc finger protein ZEB1 represses miR-200 family members, facilitating epithelial-mesenchymal transition and invasion [4], while REST, a neural-specific repressor, silences miR-124 and miR-137 in glioblastoma stem cells, maintaining an undifferentiated state [5]. YY1, another key regulator, suppresses miR-7 expression, leading to elevated EGFR signaling [6]. Additionally, STAT3 directly activates miR-21 and miR-181b, reinforcing survival pathways and chemoresistance [7]. These transcriptional networks are often dysregulated by upstream oncogenic signals, including EGFR/PI3K/AKT and JAK/STAT pathways, creating feed-forward loops that lock cells into a malignant state.

Emerging evidence highlights the role of lineage-specific factors such as SOX2 and OCT4 in sustaining miRNA expression profiles that favor stemness. SOX2 binds to enhancers of the miR-17-92 cluster and represses miR-145, while OCT4 suppresses miR-34a, jointly promoting self-renewal [8]. The interplay between these transcription factors and epigenetic modifiers further stabilizes miRNA dysregulation, making them attractive therapeutic targets.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNAs as Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Circulating microRNAs in blood and cerebrospinal fluid
subsections.content:
Circulating microRNAs in blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) have emerged as promising non-invasive biomarkers for glioblastoma detection and monitoring. Due to their stability in biofluids and ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, microRNAs released by tumor cells via exosomes or protein complexes can be detected in serum, plasma, and CSF. Studies have demonstrated distinct microRNA profiles in glioblastoma patients compared to healthy controls or those with low-grade gliomas, with elevated levels of miR-21, miR-10b, and miR-155 consistently observed in plasma and serum samples. CSF, being in direct contact with the tumor microenvironment, often reveals more tumor-specific signatures, including upregulated miR-21 and downregulated miR-128, with higher sensitivity than blood-based assays in some cohorts.

Recent work has validated the diagnostic potential of microRNA panels in distinguishing glioblastoma from other neurological conditions. For instance, a five-miRNA signature in CSF (miR-21, miR-10b, miR-155, miR-196a, miR-221) achieved high accuracy in identifying glioblastoma patients, even in early-stage disease. Moreover, longitudinal studies show that circulating miR-21 levels correlate with tumor burden and response to therapy, suggesting utility in treatment monitoring. The differential abundance of microRNAs in CSF versus blood also supports their compartment-specific roles, with CSF-derived signatures offering superior specificity for intracranial tumors.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNAs as Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA signatures for molecular subtypes (e.g., proneural, mesenchymal)
subsections.content:
MicroRNA signatures have been instrumental in distinguishing molecular subtypes of glioblastoma, particularly the proneural, mesenchymal, and classical subtypes defined by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). The proneural subtype is characterized by elevated expression of miR-128, miR-124, and miR-137, which promote neuronal differentiation and suppress stemness by targeting BMI1, E2F3, and SOX2, respectively. In contrast, the mesenchymal subtype exhibits upregulation of miR-21, miR-155, and miR-10b, which drive pro-inflammatory signaling, EMT-like transitions, and invasion through NF-κB and STAT3 activation. A multi-miRNA panel including miR-21, miR-155, and miR-221 has been shown to robustly classify mesenchymal tumors with high accuracy, correlating with poor prognosis and therapy resistance.

Systematic profiling of tumor and circulating miRNAs has revealed subtype-specific signatures that mirror intratumoral heterogeneity. For instance, miR-181d is selectively downregulated in the mesenchymal subtype and correlates with MGMT methylation status, while miR-10a is enriched in proneural tumors and linked to HOX gene dysregulation. Exosomal miRNA profiles in plasma and CSF further reflect these subtypes, enabling non-invasive molecular stratification. Notably, a 5-miRNA signature (miR-21, miR-155, miR-181d, miR-128, and miR-124) has been validated to distinguish proneural from mesenchymal glioblastoma with high sensitivity and specificity in independent cohorts.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNAs as Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Prognostic value of individual and panel-based microRNA expression
subsections.content:
Individual microRNAs have demonstrated significant prognostic value in glioblastoma, with dysregulated expression correlating strongly with survival outcomes. For instance, low expression of miR-181d is associated with improved overall survival and enhanced sensitivity to temozolomide, likely through its regulation of MGMT and other DNA repair genes. Similarly, elevated levels of miR-21, while already established as a diagnostic marker, also predict shorter progression-free and overall survival, reinforcing its role as a dual diagnostic-prognostic indicator. In contrast, tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-128 and miR-34a are frequently downregulated in aggressive tumors, and their loss correlates with stemness, therapy resistance, and poor prognosis.

Panel-based microRNA signatures offer enhanced prognostic power by integrating multiple biomarkers to capture tumor heterogeneity. A seven-miRNA signature (miR-10b, miR-21, miR-128, miR-181d, miR-221, miR-222, and miR-342) was shown to stratify patients into distinct risk groups with significant survival differences, outperforming single-miRNA models. Another study identified a four-miRNA panel (miR-10b, miR-21, miR-128, and miR-181d) in plasma that independently predicted survival after adjusting for age, IDH status, and MGMT methylation. These multi-miRNA signatures often reflect coordinated dysregulation of key pathways including apoptosis, cell cycle, and stemness maintenance.

Importantly, prognostic miRNA panels have been validated in independent cohorts and remain predictive even in the context of standard therapies, suggesting clinical utility beyond conventional biomarkers. Integration of miRNA profiles with genomic and epigenetic data further refines risk stratification, positioning microRNAs as dynamic, non-invasive tools for personalized prognosis in glioblastoma.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNAs as Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Comparison with traditional biomarkers (e.g., IDH1, MGMT)
subsections.content:
The prognostic and diagnostic utility of microRNAs in glioblastoma is increasingly evaluated in comparison to established molecular biomarkers such as IDH1 mutation status and MGMT promoter methylation. While IDH1 mutations define a distinct glioblastoma subtype with significantly better prognosis, microRNA signatures have demonstrated independent prognostic power in IDH1-wildtype tumors, suggesting complementary rather than redundant roles. For instance, a seven-microRNA signature was shown to predict survival independently of both IDH1 and MGMT status, offering refined risk stratification beyond conventional markers ref [18]. Similarly, MGMT methylation remains the strongest predictor of temozolomide response, yet microRNA-181d directly targets MGMT mRNA and correlates with chemosensitivity even in MGMT-unmethylated cases, indicating functional interplay ref [49]. Recent studies have integrated microRNA expression profiles with IDH1 and MGMT data to improve predictive accuracy, revealing that combinatorial models outperform single biomarkers in survival prediction ref [44]. Moreover, circulating microRNAs can be dynamically monitored during treatment, unlike static genomic or epigenetic markers, enabling real-time assessment of tumor evolution and therapeutic resistance.

Unlike IDH1 mutations, which are largely stable and early events, microRNA expression is highly responsive to microenvironmental cues and therapy, offering a more dynamic readout. Plasma-based microRNA panels have been validated to predict overall survival with comparable or superior sensitivity to MGMT methylation in multivariate analyses ref [17]. Furthermore, microRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155 are upregulated in both MGMT-methylated and unmethylated tumors, suggesting broader relevance across molecular subtypes. The ability of microRNAs to reflect tumor heterogeneity and stemness properties—unlike IDH1 or MGMT, which are binary markers—enhances their potential as multiplexed biomarkers for precision oncology.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA mimics and synthetic analogs for tumor-suppressor replacement
subsections.content:
Restoration of tumor-suppressive microRNAs via synthetic mimics represents a promising therapeutic strategy in glioblastoma. MicroRNA mimics, designed to replicate endogenous tumor-suppressive miRNAs, have been shown to inhibit proliferation, induce apoptosis, and suppress stemness in glioblastoma cells. For instance, delivery of miR-34a mimics suppresses NOTCH1 and MET signaling, reducing glioblastoma stem cell self-renewal and tumor growth in preclinical models. Similarly, reintroduction of miR-128 mimics targets BMI1 and E2F3, promoting differentiation and inhibiting cell cycle progression. MiR-145 mimics have also demonstrated efficacy by downregulating OCT4 and SOX2, key pluripotency factors in glioma stem cells. Synthetic analogs of miR-7, which targets EGFR and IRS-1/2, have been shown to attenuate oncogenic signaling and sensitize tumors to therapy. These mimics are often engineered with chemical modifications to enhance stability and reduce off-target effects.

Preclinical studies have further validated the therapeutic potential of miR-181 family mimics, which restore sensitivity to temozolomide by modulating BCL2 and MCL1 expression. Additionally, miR-124 mimics, whose expression is epigenetically silenced in glioblastoma, have been shown to reverse stem-like properties and inhibit tumor growth in orthotopic models. Despite their promise, systemic delivery remains challenging due to the blood-brain barrier and rapid nuclease degradation, necessitating advanced delivery platforms for clinical translation.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: AntagomiRs and locked nucleic acids (LNAs) against oncomiRs
subsections.content:
AntagomiRs and locked nucleic acid (LNA)-modified oligonucleotides represent potent strategies for inhibiting oncogenic microRNAs (oncomiRs) in glioblastoma. AntagomiRs, chemically modified antisense oligonucleotides complementary to target miRNAs, effectively sequester and neutralize oncomiRs such as miR-21 and miR-10b, which are consistently overexpressed in glioblastoma and drive proliferation, invasion, and therapy resistance. LNAs, with their high-affinity binding and nuclease resistance, enable precise and durable suppression of oncomiRs at low doses. For instance, LNA-mediated inhibition of miR-21 significantly reduces tumor growth and enhances temozolomide sensitivity in preclinical glioblastoma models by restoring expression of PTEN and PDCD4. Similarly, antagomiR-10b treatment suppresses invasion and metastasis in orthotopic models by derepressing HOXD10 and other metastasis suppressors.

Targeting miR-221/222 with LNAs has been shown to inhibit cell cycle progression and restore p27Kip1 and p57Kip2 expression, thereby reducing glioblastoma stem cell viability. Moreover, systemic delivery of LNA-anti-miR-155 attenuates STAT3 activation and tumor-associated inflammation, improving survival in murine glioblastoma models. These approaches demonstrate that selective oncomiR inhibition can reverse key oncogenic pathways without broad cytotoxicity, offering a promising therapeutic avenue. Recent studies have further validated the efficacy of LNA-modified inhibitors in crossing the blood-brain barrier when conjugated to targeting ligands, enhancing their translational potential.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Nanoparticle-based delivery systems for blood-brain barrier penetration
subsections.content:
Effective therapeutic modulation of microRNAs in glioblastoma requires overcoming the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which severely limits the delivery of oligonucleotide-based agents. Nanoparticle-based systems have emerged as promising platforms to facilitate transcytosis across the BBB while protecting microRNA therapeutics from degradation. Lipid-based nanoparticles, particularly those coated with transferrin or lactoferrin, exploit receptor-mediated endocytosis to enhance brain uptake, as demonstrated in orthotopic glioblastoma models where targeted delivery of miR-34a mimics suppressed tumor growth and extended survival ref [79]. Polymeric nanoparticles composed of PLGA or chitosan, functionalized with peptides such as Angiopep-2, have also shown enhanced BBB penetration and efficient intracellular delivery of antagomiRs against miR-21 and miR-10b, resulting in significant tumor regression ref [80]. Exosome-mimetic nanovesicles derived from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry tumor-suppressive miRNAs, leveraging their natural homing properties to glioma cells ref [81]. Additionally, gold nanoparticles conjugated with LNA-anti-miR-155 have enabled controlled release and reduced off-target effects in preclinical models ref [82].

Recent advances include the use of dendrimers and silica-based nanoparticles with surface modifications that enhance BBB permeability and reduce immune clearance. For instance, PEGylated dendrimers loaded with miR-128 mimics demonstrated improved biodistribution and tumor accumulation compared to free oligonucleotides ref [83]. Similarly, lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles co-delivering temozolomide and miR-181d sensitized resistant glioblastoma cells by simultaneously restoring chemosensitivity and suppressing MGMT ref [84]. In vivo studies using intranasal delivery of miRNA-loaded nanoparticles have bypassed the BBB entirely, achieving therapeutic concentrations in the brain parenchyma with minimal systemic exposure ref [85]. These systems are increasingly being optimized for dual targeting—combining BBB penetration with glioma-specific ligands such as transferrin receptor antibodies or EGFR-binding peptides—to maximize tumor specificity and minimize neurotoxicity ref [86].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNAs in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Combination therapies with radiation and chemotherapy
subsections.content:
Combination therapies integrating microRNA modulation with conventional radiation and chemotherapy have emerged as a promising strategy to overcome therapeutic resistance in glioblastoma. Restoration of tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-181d, which targets MGMT, has been shown to sensitize glioblastoma cells to temozolomide, enhancing DNA damage and apoptosis in preclinical models. Similarly, inhibition of oncogenic miR-21 with locked nucleic acid antagonists restores PTEN expression and synergizes with radiation to suppress tumor growth and improve survival in orthotopic models. Co-delivery systems combining temozolomide with miR-181d in lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles have demonstrated enhanced chemosensitivity and reduced tumor recurrence compared to monotherapies. Furthermore, miR-34a replacement has been shown to potentiate the effects of radiation by downregulating NOTCH1 and MET, key mediators of radioresistance in glioblastoma stem cells. Targeted delivery of antagomiR-155 has also been reported to reduce inflammation and enhance the efficacy of radiotherapy by suppressing STAT3 signaling. These combinatorial approaches leverage the ability of miRNAs to modulate multiple resistance pathways simultaneously, offering a multifaceted strategy to overcome the adaptive responses that limit conventional treatments.

Recent studies have further demonstrated that epigenetic modulation of miRNA expression can enhance chemoradiation sensitivity. For instance, HDAC inhibition restores expression of silenced tumor-suppressive miRNAs, including miR-128 and miR-145, which in turn sensitizes glioblastoma cells to temozolomide and radiation by targeting BMI1 and BCL2, respectively. Additionally, miR-125b repression has been shown to enhance radiation-induced apoptosis by upregulating TP53INP1, while miR-221/222 inhibition reverses cell cycle dysregulation and improves response to chemotherapy. These findings underscore the potential of miRNA-based combination therapies to re-sensitize resistant glioblastoma subpopulations and improve clinical outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Resistance Mechanisms and MicroRNA-Mediated Treatment Failure
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNAs regulating DNA repair and MGMT expression
subsections.content:
MicroRNA dysregulation significantly influences DNA repair capacity and MGMT expression in glioblastoma, contributing to temozolomide resistance. miR-181d directly targets the MGMT 3'UTR, reducing its expression and sensitizing tumor cells to alkylating agents; low miR-181d levels correlate with poor prognosis and MGMT promoter unmethylated status [1]. Similarly, miR-603 has been shown to bind the MGMT mRNA 3'UTR, suppressing its translation and enhancing chemosensitivity in vitro and in vivo [2]. Beyond MGMT, miR-128 targets the DNA repair enzyme RAD51, impairing homologous recombination and increasing genomic instability in response to DNA damage [3]. miR-181b also modulates DNA repair by downregulating ATM and ATR, key kinases in the DNA damage response pathway, thereby reducing repair efficiency and promoting cell death after irradiation or alkylating agent exposure [4].

Conversely, oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155 promote DNA repair by suppressing negative regulators of repair pathways. miR-21 targets MSH2 and MSH6, components of the mismatch repair system, leading to error tolerance and resistance to temozolomide [5]. miR-155 represses MLH1 and PMS2, further compromising mismatch repair and facilitating mutagenic survival [6]. Additionally, epigenetic silencing of tumor-suppressive miRNAs like miR-181a and miR-181c via H3K9me3 and DNA methylation contributes to sustained MGMT expression and chemoresistance in glioblastoma stem cells [7]. The coordinated repression of multiple miRNAs regulating DNA repair machinery underscores a multifaceted mechanism of therapeutic evasion, where loss of miRNA-mediated control enables persistent DNA repair and survival under genotoxic stress.

subsections.section_title: Resistance Mechanisms and MicroRNA-Mediated Treatment Failure
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA-mediated evasion of radiation-induced apoptosis
subsections.content:
MicroRNA-mediated evasion of radiation-induced apoptosis is a key mechanism of therapeutic resistance in glioblastoma. Several tumor-suppressive miRNAs are downregulated following irradiation, enabling cancer cells to evade intrinsic apoptotic pathways. For instance, loss of miR-34a, a direct p53 target, reduces BAX and PUMA expression, impairing mitochondrial apoptosis after DNA damage ref [70]. Similarly, genomic deletion of the miR-15a/16-1 cluster leads to constitutive overexpression of BCL2, conferring resistance to radiation-triggered apoptosis ref [54]. The miR-17-92 cluster, often amplified in glioblastoma, promotes survival by repressing pro-apoptotic BIM and E2F1 regulators, thereby blunting the apoptotic response to ionizing radiation ref [13]. Additionally, miR-21, frequently upregulated post-radiation, suppresses multiple apoptotic mediators including APAF1 and CASPASE-3, directly inhibiting caspase activation ref [5].

Conversely, oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-221/222 are induced by radiation and target the cell cycle inhibitor p27Kip1 and the pro-apoptotic protein PTEN, enhancing survival signaling ref [10]. The miR-106b-25 cluster, homologous to miR-17-92, similarly inhibits apoptosis by targeting BIM and suppressing the p21-mediated cell cycle arrest pathway ref [87]. Furthermore, epigenetic silencing of miR-124 and miR-137, which normally promote apoptosis via regulation of CDK6 and SUZ12, is exacerbated by radiation, contributing to sustained stemness and resistance ref [6]. These coordinated miRNA alterations create a permissive environment for tumor cell survival despite genotoxic stress, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets to restore radiation sensitivity.

subsections.section_title: Resistance Mechanisms and MicroRNA-Mediated Treatment Failure
subsections.subsection_title: Adaptive microRNA reprogramming during treatment
subsections.content:
Glioblastoma cells exhibit dynamic microRNA reprogramming in response to therapeutic stress, enabling adaptive survival and resistance. Upon temozolomide exposure, tumor cells upregulate oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155, which suppress pro-apoptotic genes and enhance DNA repair capacity, while downregulating tumor-suppressive miRNAs like miR-128 and miR-34a to maintain stemness and evade cell cycle arrest. This reprogramming is often mediated by transcription factors activated under therapy-induced stress, including NF-κB and STAT3, which transcriptionally modulate miRNA expression networks. Longitudinal profiling of patient samples reveals that miRNA signatures shift significantly during treatment cycles, with specific clusters associated with recurrence and poor response. For instance, miR-10b is induced post-radiation to promote invasion and survival, while miR-125b is upregulated to repress TP53INP1 and sustain stem cell properties under therapeutic pressure. Epigenetic mechanisms, including histone methylation and DNA methylation, further stabilize these adaptive changes, locking cells into a resistant state. Exosomal transfer of reprogrammed miRNAs between tumor cells and the microenvironment also facilitates systemic resistance, as demonstrated by the secretion of miR-1246 and miR-21 in extracellular vesicles that reprogram macrophages and astrocytes to support tumor persistence.

Emerging evidence indicates that adaptive miRNA shifts are not random but follow coordinated regulatory patterns. The miR-17-92 cluster, previously implicated in tumorigenesis, is further amplified under chemotherapy to enhance anti-apoptotic signaling, while the miR-106b-25 cluster is upregulated to suppress E2F1-mediated cell death. These changes are often accompanied by global suppression of miRNA biogenesis machinery, such as Dicer and Drosha, which selectively favors the retention of oncogenic miRNAs over tumor-suppressive ones. Single-cell RNA sequencing of treated glioblastoma xenografts confirms heterogeneous miRNA expression profiles, suggesting that subpopulations with distinct adaptive signatures survive and repopulate the tumor. Targeting these dynamic networks—such as inhibiting miR-10b or restoring miR-128—has shown promise in preclinical models to reverse acquired resistance.

subsections.section_title: Resistance Mechanisms and MicroRNA-Mediated Treatment Failure
subsections.subsection_title: Cross-talk with alternative signaling pathways (e.g., EGFR, PI3K/AKT)
subsections.content:
MicroRNA dysregulation in glioblastoma frequently intersects with key oncogenic signaling pathways, particularly EGFR and PI3K/AKT, creating feed-forward loops that sustain therapy resistance. For instance, miR-7 directly targets EGFR and IRS-1/2, and its downregulation—mediated by the transcription factor YY1—leads to hyperactivation of both EGFR and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling, promoting survival and chemoresistance ref [34]. Conversely, the PI3K/AKT pathway transcriptionally upregulates oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155, which further suppress PTEN and other negative regulators, amplifying pathway activity ref [35]. The miR-17-92 cluster, frequently amplified in glioblastoma, targets PTEN and BIM, thereby enhancing PI3K/AKT signaling and inhibiting apoptosis ref [14]. Additionally, miR-10b has been shown to activate PI3K/AKT by repressing HOXD10, a negative regulator of this pathway, contributing to invasion and treatment evasion ref [2].

Cross-talk is further evident in the regulation of feedback inhibitors; miR-126 targets PIK3R2, a regulatory subunit of PI3K, and its loss in glioblastoma enhances AKT activation ref [71]. Meanwhile, miR-143 suppresses KRAS and ERK signaling, and its epigenetic silencing indirectly potentiates PI3K/AKT activity ref [77]. Exosomal transfer of miR-21 from tumor cells to stromal compartments activates PI3K/AKT in recipient cells, fostering a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment ref [53]. These interactions underscore that microRNA-mediated rewiring of EGFR and PI3K/AKT signaling is not merely correlative but functionally central to adaptive resistance, suggesting that combinatorial targeting of miRNAs and these pathways may be necessary to overcome therapeutic failure.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Future Directions, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Heterogeneity and tumor plasticity complicating microRNA targeting
subsections.content:
Glioblastoma's profound intratumoral heterogeneity and adaptive plasticity pose significant challenges to microRNA-based therapeutics, as distinct subclones exhibit divergent miRNA expression profiles that evolve under therapeutic pressure. Single-cell analyses reveal spatially segregated populations with unique miRNA signatures, including differential expression of miR-21, miR-155, and miR-128 across tumor core, invasive margin, and stem cell niches, undermining the efficacy of pan-tumor targeting strategies [1]. Tumor plasticity, driven by epigenetic reprogramming and microenvironmental cues, enables dynamic shifts in miRNA networks that promote therapy resistance and phenotypic switching between stem-like and differentiated states [2]. For instance, hypoxia-induced upregulation of miR-210 and downregulation of miR-34a facilitate metabolic adaptation and stemness maintenance, rendering miRNA replacement or inhibition context-dependent [3]. Moreover, lineage tracing studies demonstrate that miRNA expression can be transiently altered during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition or in response to radiation, leading to rapid escape from miRNA-targeted interventions [4]. The coexistence of miRNA-deficient and miRNA-overexpressing subpopulations within the same tumor further complicates the design of universal miRNA modulators, as targeting one subclone may inadvertently select for resistant variants [5].

Recent evidence suggests that non-cell-autonomous signaling via exosomal miRNAs contributes to heterogeneity by redistributing oncogenic or tumor-suppressive miRNAs across subclones, effectively creating a coordinated, yet heterogeneous, regulatory network [6]. For example, glioblastoma stem cells secrete exosomes enriched in miR-1246, which reprograms neighboring cells toward a more aggressive phenotype, blurring the boundaries between molecular subtypes [7]. Additionally, the plasticity of miRNA biogenesis machinery—such as variable expression of Dicer, Drosha, and Exportin-5 across tumor regions—further amplifies spatial and temporal miRNA dysregulation [8]. These dynamics necessitate a shift from static miRNA targeting to adaptive, context-aware therapeutic approaches that account for tumor evolution and microenvironmental feedback loops [9].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Future Directions, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Standardization of detection methods and data normalization
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity of microRNA detection methods across studies impedes reproducibility and meta-analyses in glioblastoma research. Variations in sample collection (e.g., tissue vs. plasma vs. CSF), RNA extraction protocols, and platform selection (qRT-PCR, microarrays, RNA-seq) introduce significant technical bias, confounding biomarker discovery and validation efforts. Standardization of pre-analytical variables—such as sample storage conditions, hemolysis control in biofluids, and normalization strategies—is critical for reliable miRNA quantification. For instance, the choice of reference genes for qRT-PCR normalization remains contentious, with commonly used small nucleolar RNAs (e.g., U6, SNORD44) showing variable stability in glioblastoma samples, leading to inaccurate relative quantification [1].

Data normalization in high-throughput sequencing is further complicated by differences in library preparation, sequencing depth, and bioinformatic pipelines. Studies have demonstrated that global mean normalization, quantile normalization, and spike-in controls yield divergent results when applied to miRNA-seq data from glioblastoma cohorts, affecting downstream differential expression analyses [2]. The absence of consensus on reference miRNAs or external controls for CSF and plasma samples exacerbates inter-laboratory variability [3]. Moreover, the presence of exosomal and protein-bound miRNAs in biofluids introduces additional layers of complexity, as different isolation methods (ultracentrifugation, precipitation, immunoaffinity) enrich distinct subpopulations [4].

Recent efforts have proposed standardized workflows, such as the MIQE guidelines adapted for miRNA studies, and the use of synthetic spike-ins for normalization in circulating miRNA profiling [5]. A multi-center validation study demonstrated improved consistency in miRNA signatures when using a panel of stably expressed miRNAs (e.g., miR-16, miR-191) across glioblastoma plasma samples, though tissue-specific stability remains an open challenge [6]. The development of digital PCR and single-molecule sequencing platforms offers promise for absolute quantification, reducing reliance on relative normalization [7]. However, widespread adoption requires coordinated efforts among consortia such as the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) to enforce uniform protocols [8].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Future Directions, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Preclinical-to-clinical translation gaps
subsections.content:
The translation of microRNA-based therapeutics from preclinical models to clinical applications in glioblastoma remains hindered by fundamental biological and technical disparities. Most preclinical studies rely on immunocompromised mouse models that fail to recapitulate the human immune microenvironment, limiting the predictive value of immune-modulatory miRNA interventions such as those targeting miR-155 or miR-21 ref [13]. Additionally, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely restricts systemic delivery of miRNA mimics or inhibitors, and while nanoparticle strategies show promise in rodents, their scalability and safety in humans remain unproven ref [49]. Many studies use supraphysiological dosing or non-clinical delivery routes (e.g., intracranial injection) that are not translatable to patients, undermining clinical relevance ref [74]. Furthermore, the heterogeneity of human glioblastoma is inadequately modeled in cell line-derived xenografts, which lack the spatial and cellular diversity observed in patient tumors ref [92].

Clinical trials of miRNA therapeutics in glioblastoma have been sparse and largely unsuccessful due to poor pharmacokinetics, off-target effects, and insufficient tumor penetration. For instance, early-phase trials of LNA-anti-miR-21 showed limited bioavailability and no significant survival benefit despite robust preclinical efficacy ref [45]. The absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers to confirm target engagement in the human brain further complicates dose optimization ref [27]. Moreover, the dynamic reprogramming of miRNA networks under therapeutic pressure, as observed in temozolomide-resistant clones, suggests that single-miRNA targeting may be insufficient to overcome adaptive resistance ref [54]. Finally, regulatory pathways for miRNA-based drugs remain ill-defined, with no standardized framework for manufacturing, quality control, or long-term safety assessment in neuro-oncology.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Future Directions, and Clinical Translation
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging technologies: CRISPR-based microRNA editing and single-cell miRNA profiling
subsections.content:
CRISPR-based technologies have emerged as powerful tools for precise microRNA editing in glioblastoma, enabling targeted knockout, knock-in, or modulation of miRNA loci with unprecedented specificity. CRISPR-Cas9 has been used to delete oncogenic miRNA clusters such as miR-17-92, resulting in reduced tumor growth and enhanced sensitivity to chemotherapy in preclinical models. Similarly, CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) has been employed to repress miR-21 expression without altering genomic sequence, thereby restoring PTEN and PDCD4 tumor suppressor activity. These approaches overcome limitations of antisense oligonucleotides by enabling permanent, heritable modifications in tumor cells and their progeny.

Complementing genetic editing, single-cell miRNA profiling has revolutionized the characterization of intratumoral heterogeneity by resolving miRNA expression at individual cell resolution. Recent advances in droplet-based sequencing and barcoding techniques now permit simultaneous detection of miRNAs and mRNAs in single glioblastoma cells, revealing distinct miRNA signatures in stem-like, differentiated, and immune-interacting subpopulations. This has uncovered rare, therapy-resistant clones with unique miRNA profiles that evade bulk sequencing detection. Integration of single-cell miRNA data with spatial transcriptomics further maps miRNA expression gradients across tumor niches, linking microenvironmental cues to miRNA-driven plasticity.
